blocks.text: In damped oscillation the amplitude decreases with time, but it can be kept constant by applying a periodic external force called a driving force. When an oscillating body is acted on by a periodic driving force, the oscillation is a forced oscillation and its frequency is the driving frequency; the vibration of a vehicle caused by its running engine is an example. In forced oscillation, the amplitude depends on the relation between the driving frequency and the natural frequency of the body.

blocks.title: Resonance
blocks.text: When the frequency of the driving force is the same as the natural frequency of the oscillating body, the amplitude of vibration becomes very large. This is resonance.
The book adds that resonance also occurs when the applied frequency is a whole-number multiple of the natural frequency: if f1 is the natural frequency, at f2 = 2f1, f3 = 3f1, ... fn = nf1.

blocks.title: Which systems resonate at multiples
blocks.text: A simple pendulum or a mass on a spring has only one natural frequency, so it resonates only when driven at that frequency. Systems such as stretched strings and air columns have a whole series of natural frequencies, f1, 2f1, 3f1 and so on, and they can resonate at each of them. The statement about multiples applies to such systems.

Demonstration (Fig 14.17): pendulums A and B of length l1 and C and D of length l2 hang from a horizontal rod, together with a pendulum P whose length can be set to l1 or l2. With P at length l1, its vibration reaches the others through the rod. A and B receive a driving force at their own natural frequency, so their amplitude grows by resonance, while C and D, whose natural frequencies differ from P's, hardly move. If P is made of length l2, C and D resonate while A and B stay nearly at rest.

blocks.alt: A horizontal rod between two stands carries five pendulums: P (green, length l1, the driver), A and B (purple, length l1) and C and D (red, the shorter length l2). Dashed lines show P, A and B swinging with large amplitude, while C and D hang still. A note explains that A and B resonate because they have the same length as P.
blocks.caption: Resonance with coupled pendulums (original diagram after Fig 14.17).
blocks.long_description: Every pendulum receives the same small pushes through the rod, but only those whose natural frequency matches the driver build up a large swing.

blocks.title: Interesting information
blocks.text: During an earthquake, seismic waves can set buildings oscillating. On 8 October 2005 an earthquake of magnitude 7.6 struck Azad Jammu and Kashmir, centred near Muzaffarabad; over 86,000 people died. (The book prints 'reactor scale'; earthquake magnitude is measured on the Richter or moment-magnitude scale.)
Circumstances in which resonance is useful

items: Heating food in a microwave oven: the oven fills its inside with microwaves (the book gives 3-30 GHz and a wavelength of about 12 cm; household ovens use about 2.45 GHz). The rapidly changing field makes the water molecules in food oscillate and collide, and this energy becomes heat. Plastic or glass containers hardly heat up because they contain no water (the book's Fig 14.18 is a photograph of an oven).

Radio tuning: turning the tuning knob of an analogue radio changes the natural frequency of the receiver's electrical circuit. When it equals the frequency of a station, resonance occurs, the energy absorbed from that station is greatest, and that is the station we hear (Fig 14.19 is a photograph of a radio).

blocks.text: Circumstances in which resonance should be avoided

items: Bridge vibration: soldiers are told to break step while crossing a bridge. If they marched in step, the frequency of their footsteps could equal the natural frequency of the bridge, setting it vibrating with a large amplitude so that it might collapse.
Aeroplane wings: the wings experience aerodynamic forces, turbulence and engine vibration. If the frequency of these forces matches the natural frequency of the wings, resonance can be dangerous.

blocks.title: Interesting information
blocks.text: The frequency at which an object naturally oscillates is called its resonant frequency. The sound board of a piano, violin or guitar resonates with the vibrating string, amplifying the sound into a louder, richer note. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) uses strong radio-frequency radiation to make nuclei oscillate; the pattern of energy absorbed produces a computer-enhanced image. The amplitude of a swing grows when it is pushed at its natural frequency.

blocks.prompt: Why are soldiers told to break step when crossing a bridge?
blocks.explanation: Marching in step applies a periodic force; if its frequency matched the bridge's natural frequency, resonance could build up a dangerously large amplitude.

items: Resonance: driving frequency = natural frequency gives a very large amplitude.
Useful: microwave ovens, radio tuning, musical instruments, MRI.
To avoid: marching on bridges, aircraft wings, buildings in earthquakes.
